annotation: It treated the filer as a qualifying surviving spouse even though that status requires a dependent child. So it used the joint $32,000/$44,000 Social Security thresholds, which gave $11,542 of taxable benefits instead of $18,542, and the joint $32,300 standard deduction plus a $1,650 aged add-on. Filing single, AGI is $50,437; subtracting $18,341 of itemized deductions and the $6,000 senior deduction leaves $26,096 taxable and $2,883 of tax in the 10% and 12% brackets.

It computed $18,542 of taxable Social Security and $50,436 of AGI correctly, then applied the joint $32,200 standard deduction and $1,650 aged add-on for a surviving spouse. Qualifying-surviving-spouse status requires a dependent child, so the filer is single. As a single filer, $18,341 of itemized deductions plus the $6,000 senior deduction leaves $26,096 taxable, with part of it in the 12% bracket.

It counted the $48,000 of nontaxable veterans benefits as gross income and taxed 85% of Social Security without the provisional-income formula. It also subtracted employer insurance premiums with no wages to subtract them from, then dropped its own roughly $6,600 estimate and asserted zero. The correct figures are AGI of $50,437 (including $18,542 of taxable Social Security) minus $18,341 itemized and the $6,000 senior deduction, which leaves $26,096 taxable and $2,883 of tax.

It chose single status correctly but got the second tier of the Social Security formula wrong: it added half of benefits ($13,048) where the formula uses the lesser of that or $4,500. That made the full 85% cap of $22,182 taxable instead of $18,542 and overstated AGI by $3,640. It also took the $18,150 standard deduction plus aged add-on instead of the larger $18,341 itemized total (real estate taxes plus Texas sales tax).

It used joint qualifying-surviving-spouse deductions even though there is no dependent child, set taxable Social Security to the 85% cap without the tiered formula, and capped SALT at $10,000 although the 2026 cap is $40,400. The model named the correct SSI-related aged pathway but asserted rather than computed the SSI income test: applying the $20 general exclusion, the $65 earned-income exclusion, and the one-half earned-income disregard gives countable income of about $15,205 from Social Security plus about $14,500 from wages, roughly $2,475 per month, far above the couple SSI federal benefit rate and above Virginia's ~80% FPL aged/blind/disabled limit, which is why SSI received is 0 and medicaid_category is NONE. It compounded this by treating Medicare Savings Program status (QMB/SLMB) and medically needy spend-down as Medicaid-eligibility categories, neither of which is a qualifying pathway here, and by never noticing that household income at 2.05x FPL exceeds even the 100% FPL QMB test.

Because SSI is 0, no category attaches and medicaid_category resolves to NONE despite the head being 71.

The model supplied no rule at all and defaulted age 71 to Medicaid eligibility. Age 71 removes the head from the MAGI expansion adult group (which ends at 64) and routes eligibility to the SSI-linked aged pathway, whose income and asset tests this household fails, so the correct derivation yields no qualifying category; the model's answer is consistent with an age-alone heuristic that skips every income test.

The model equated Medicare Savings Program status with Medicaid eligibility, concluding the head qualifies "as a Medicare savings program recipient"; MSP buy-in is not a PolicyEngine Medicaid eligibility category, and the head qualifies through none of the actual pathways. It also mischaracterized $44,289 of combined wages and Social Security as low income when that is 2.05x FPL, above both the MAGI thresholds and the 100% FPL QMB limit it implicitly relied on.

The SSI-related aged/blind/disabled test counts the couple's combined countable income under spousal deeming, not the spouse's zero personal earnings, and Virginia's ABD standard of roughly 80% FPL (about $17,300 for two) is failed by $44,289 by a factor of 2.5; with $0 SSI received, the SSI-recipient route is closed as well.

The model identified the correct pathway, Virginia's aged/blind/disabled category, but misstated its income limit, claiming $15,225 of Social Security plus $29,064 of wages sits 'well under the ABD income and resource limits for a couple after standard disregards.' Virginia's ABD categorically needy standard is about 80% FPL (roughly $17,300 annually for a couple), and the SSI disregards ($20 general, $65 plus half the remainder on earnings) still leave about $29,100 of countable annual income, so the couple fails the income test by more than $10,000; the resource check the model relied on is irrelevant once income disqualifies.

No Medicaid category is conferred by age alone: the 65+ non-MAGI route requires SSI receipt or countable income within the state's SSI-related ABD standard (about 80% FPL) plus the $3,000 couple resource limit, and with $0 SSI and $44,289 of household income the engine assigns medicaid_category = NONE.

MSP premium assistance is not a Medicaid eligibility category here, and the household fails it regardless: the QMB limit is 100% FPL while this couple sits at 2.05x FPL. The model also called the 69-year-old 'eligible for Medicare soon' when Medicare eligibility attached at 65, and it never applied any income test to the actual aged/blind/disabled pathway.

Under the requested PolicyEngine rule, the spouse's age of 69 satisfies the age-65 Medicare eligibility criterion, so the unlisted work history does not change the result.
